CONTEXT: You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ "inflection" library (Rails-style Inflector) purely as a black box.
BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test11_executable   (run from any cwd; it needs no files)
USAGE: ./test11_executable <int num> <word>    -- requires argc > 2, then prints exactly 11 lines.
LINE MAP (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  ordinalize(num)
  3  camelize(word, true)
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  titleize(word)
  6  capitalize(word)
  7  truncate(word, 5)
  8  truncate(word, 10, "~")
  9  parameterize(word)
  10 parameterize(word, "_")
  11 isPlural(word)  -> prints 0 or 1
HOW TO PROBE ONE LINE:
  /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1 'my_word' | sed -n '3p'
Use single quotes or printf to control argv exactly. To probe words containing spaces, quotes, newlines, backslashes, or
non-ASCII UTF-8, pass them as a SINGLE argv element (e.g. "$(printf 'a\tb')" or 'héllo'). Empty word: '' (still argc>2).

ALREADY ESTABLISHED — treat as given, do NOT spend probes re-deriving:
  * pluralize(w) = w + "s", UNLESS w exactly (case-sensitively) equals one of the uncountables
      {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}  -> then w unchanged.
      (The library's 17 plural regex rules are dead code: the first registered rule /$/ -> "s" always matches first.)
  * isPlural(w) == (singularize(w) != w).  isSingular(w) == !isPlural(w).
  * The library registers 23 singular regex rules (Rails standard) plus a first rule /s$/ -> "" ; first match wins,
    iterating in registration order. There are NO irregular() pairs and NO human() rules (person->persons, child->childs).
  * An acronyms table exists containing exactly: HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API.
  * Other literals in the binary: "..." (truncate default omission), "-" (parameterize default sep), "_", " ", "::",
    "_id", "id", "th", "st", "nd", "rd".
  * The C++ is compiled with gcc-12, uses std::regex (ECMAScript grammar) and std::string (byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness).

OPTIONAL EXTRA TOOL: you may disassemble to resolve ambiguity (objdump and nm are at /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/, on PATH).
  objdump -dC --start-address=0xADDR --stop-address=0xADDR2 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
  Symbol addresses: pluralize 0x405d12, singularize 0x405f84, camelize 0x406262, underscore 0x40636e, classify 0x40649a,
  tableize 0x40650a, humanize 0x406576, titleize 0x4066fe, ordinalize 0x40681c, dasherize 0x406992, parameterize 0x406a1a,
  isPlural 0x406bc0, isSingular 0x406c0c, upcase 0x406c2a, downcase 0x406cea, capitalize 0x406daa, decapitalize 0x406ed0,
  truncate 0x406f98, demodulize 0x40705a, deconstantize 0x4070c8, foreign_key 0x40716e, ordinal 0x4071e8, initialize 0x403cd4.
  Disassembly is a tiebreaker; observed behavior is the ground truth.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
  * Do NOT write, create, or modify any file anywhere. Read-only + running the binary only. Never touch /output.
  * Run many probes (aim 40-80). Batch them in for-loops so it is cheap. Quote carefully.
  * Adversarially attack your own hypothesis: for every rule you state, try to find an input that breaks it.
  * The goal is a byte-exact Rust reimplementation using only std. Where behavior is byte-oriented rather than
    char-oriented (UTF-8 multibyte input), say so explicitly, because Rust's String indexing would panic there.


=== ADVERSARIAL RE-DERIVATION: camelize ===
Another engineer produced the spec below for this area. Your job is to BREAK it. Assume it is subtly wrong until proven
otherwise. Design probes specifically targeting its blind spots, boundary conditions, and any place it hand-waved.
Run at least 40 fresh probes of your own against the binary. Then report the CORRECTED, complete spec.
If the spec is right, say so explicitly and state which of its claims you independently confirmed with which probes.

--- SPEC UNDER TEST ---
camelize(word: &str/&[u8], lower_first: bool) -> bytes

CONFIRMED by disassembly at 0x406262 (in-place mutation of a copy) AND by a 250-case
randomized differential test (0 mismatches). The C++ source is exactly:

  std::string camelize(const std::string& s, bool lowerFirst) {
      std::string result = s;              // byte-for-byte copy
      bool cap = !lowerFirst;              // xor 0x1  (see 0x40628f)
      size_t i = 0;
      while (i < result.size()) {          // size() re-read EVERY iteration
          if (result[i] == '_') {          // 0x5f, the ONLY special byte
              cap = true;
              result.erase(i, 1);          // delete the underscore
              i -= 1;                      // size_t; wraps if i==0, then +1 -> 0
          } else if (cap) {
              result[i] = (char)toupper((int)(signed char)result[i]);  // movsbl -> toupper
              cap = false;
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      return result;                       // trailing `cap` state is discarded
  }

Rust reimplementation (byte-oriented; do NOT use char indexing):

  fn camelize(word: &str, lower_first: bool) -> String {
      let mut b: Vec<u8> = word.as_bytes().to_vec();
      let mut cap = !lower_first;
      let mut i: usize = 0;
      while i < b.len() {
          if b[i] == b'_' {
              cap = true;
              b.remove(i);            // stay at same index i (do NOT advance)
              continue;               // equivalent to i -= 1; i += 1
          }
          if cap {
              if b[i].is_ascii_lowercase() { b[i] -= 32; }  // toupper, C locale
              cap = false;
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      // Safety: only ASCII a-z were changed to A-Z and only 0x5f bytes removed,
      // so UTF-8 validity is preserved => String::from_utf8(b).unwrap() is safe.
      String::from_utf8(b).unwrap()
  }

BEHAVIOURAL SPEC (all verified):
 1. The ONLY separator recognised is the ASCII underscore 0x5f. Every '_' is deleted
    and sets a "capitalize the next surviving byte" flag.
 2. '-', ' ', '.', '/', '::', ':', tab, newline, '~', digits, and every other byte are
    copied verbatim and do NOT trigger capitalization.
    camelize("my-word",false)=="My-word"; camelize("a/b_c",true)=="a/bC";
    camelize("a::b_c",true)=="a::bC". No '/'->'::' conversion (unlike Rails).
 3. NOTHING IS EVER LOWERCASED. There is no tolower call in the function.
    camelize("CamelCase",true)=="CamelCase"; camelize("UPPER",true)=="UPPER";
    camelize("UPPER_CASE",*)=="UPPERCASE"; camelize("FOO_bar",*)=="FOOBar".
    So `lower_first == true` does NOT mean "lowercase the first letter"; it means
    "do not uppercase the first letter".
 4. The bool only sets the INITIAL value of `cap` (cap = !lower_first). Consequences:
    - If the input's first byte is '_' (or the input is empty, or consists only of
      '_'), the two variants produce BYTE-IDENTICAL output, because the leading '_'
      sets cap=true regardless. camelize("_leading",true)==camelize("_leading",false)
      =="Leading".
    - Otherwise the two variants differ in AT MOST the first byte of the result, and
      only when that byte is ASCII a-z. All later bytes are identical in both variants
      (after the first non-'_' byte, cap is false in both paths).
 5. Leading underscores: consumed, next byte uppercased. "_a"->"A", "__double__"->"Double".
    Trailing underscores: simply deleted, cap flag left dangling and discarded.
    "a_"->"a"/"A", "ab_cd_"->"abCd"/"AbCd".
    Repeated internal underscores collapse: "a__b"->"aB"/"AB", "x__y__z"->"xYZ"/"XYZ".
    All-underscore input ("_", "__", "___") -> "" for both bools.
 6. Empty input -> "" for both bools.
 7. If the byte after an underscore is not an ASCII lowercase letter, it is emitted
    unchanged (toupper is identity) and cap is still cleared:
    "a_1b"->"a1b"/"A1b", "_9x"->"9x", "9_a"->"9A", "a_B"->"aB"/"AB",
    "_-x"->"-x", "_ x"->" x", "_\t"->"\t".
 8. THE ACRONYM TABLE (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) IS **NOT** CONSULTED. camelize is a
    pure byte loop with no table lookup, no regex, no acronym handling:
      html_tag      -> htmlTag      / HtmlTag
      api_key       -> apiKey       / ApiKey
      xml           -> xml          / Xml
      json_data     -> jsonData     / JsonData
      http_request  -> httpRequest  / HttpRequest
      my_html_parser-> myHtmlParser / MyHtmlParser
      HTML_tag      -> HTMLTag      / HTMLTag   (preserved only because input was upper)
      Html_tag      -> HtmlTag      / HtmlTag
      HTML/JSON/API -> unchanged for both bools
      API_KEY       -> APIKEY       / APIKEY
 9. Non-ASCII / multibyte UTF-8: purely byte-oriented. toupper is called with the byte
    SIGN-EXTENDED (movsbl), i.e. a negative int for bytes >= 0x80; under the C locale
    (the program never calls setlocale — no setlocale symbol in the binary) this is
    identity for all bytes 0x80..0xFF. Verified: "_élan"->"élan" (0xC3 unchanged),
    "Ünder_score"->"ÜnderScore", "ß_x"->"ßX", "a_émile"->"aémile"/"Aémile",
    raw "_\xe9x"->"\xe9x", "_\xff"->"\xff", "_\xd0\xb0"->"\xd0\xb0".
    Locale is irrelevant: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 with "i_i" still yields "iI"/"II"
    (dotted-I is NOT produced), so plain ASCII a-z => A-Z mapping is correct.
10. Invalid UTF-8 / lone continuation bytes pass through untouched; only 0x5f is
    removed, so a Rust implementation over &[u8] is exactly equivalent.
11. No NUL byte can be tested (argv is NUL-terminated); assume it would be an ordinary
    byte, but a Rust &str cannot contain issues here anyway.
--- CLAIMED GOTCHAS ---
lower_first=true does NOT lowercase anything. It merely skips the initial uppercasing. camelize("CamelCase", true) == "CamelCase", NOT "camelCase". Do not call to_lowercase on the first char.
The acronym table (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) is NOT used by camelize at all. Do not add acronym special-casing — html_tag must yield htmlTag/HtmlTag.
Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Never index a Rust String/str by byte offset and slice-assign; operate on Vec<u8> (or as_bytes().to_vec()) and only mutate ASCII a-z -> A-Z. Naive `s.chars()` + `to_uppercase()` breaks on multibyte input: 'é' after '_' must stay 'é' (0xC3 0xA9), not become 'É'.
toupper is called with a SIGN-EXTENDED char (movsbl) so bytes >= 0x80 arrive as negative ints; in the C locale glibc returns them unchanged. Using char::to_ascii_uppercase on the byte reproduces this; using Unicode uppercasing does not.
No setlocale is ever called, so the mapping is fixed ASCII a-z -> A-Z regardless of LC_ALL. Verified with LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8: 'i_i' -> 'iI'/'II'.
Only 0x5f ('_') is a separator. Dashes, spaces, dots, '/', '::' are NOT. Rails' camelize converts '/' to '::' — this implementation does not.
The erase-and-step-back loop uses `i -= 1` on a size_t; when i == 0 this wraps to SIZE_MAX and the following `i += 1` brings it back to 0. In Rust use `b.remove(i); continue;` (no decrement) — a literal `i -= 1` would panic on underflow in debug builds.
size() is re-evaluated each iteration, so the loop correctly shrinks as underscores are erased. Caching the length would read past the end.
Trailing underscores leave the capitalize flag set, but it is discarded — do not append or capitalize anything at the end. "a_" -> "a" / "A".
Empty input and all-underscore input return the empty string for BOTH bool values; the two variants are identical there (and whenever the first byte is '_').
Characters after the first surviving character are never case-changed unless immediately preceded by an underscore. "ZZ_zz" -> "ZZZz" for both bools.
The two bool variants can differ ONLY in the first byte of the result (and only when the input does not start with '_' and that byte is ASCII a-z). Don't assume a general-case transform between them.
Invalid UTF-8 in the input passes through byte-for-byte (only 0x5f is dropped), so an implementation over &str is fine only because the removed/changed bytes are ASCII; prefer Vec<u8> internally and unwrap from_utf8 (guaranteed valid).
--- END ---

input.spec:
VERDICT: The spec under test is CORRECT. I found ZERO deviations across ~1000 probes
(two exhaustive single-byte sweeps of 0x01..0xFF, 450 randomized differential cases against a
byte-exact Perl reference, and ~80 hand-targeted adversarial cases). Every numbered claim (1-11)
and every claimed gotcha is independently confirmed below. No corrections are needed.

=== EXACT BEHAVIOR ===

camelize(word: &[u8], lower_first: bool) -> bytes

  fn camelize(word: &str, lower_first: bool) -> String {
      let mut b: Vec<u8> = word.as_bytes().to_vec();
      let mut cap: bool = !lower_first;        // C++: cap = bool_byte ^ 0x1  (xor at 0x40628f)
      let mut i: usize = 0;
      while i < b.len() {                      // b.len() re-read every iteration
          if b[i] == b'_' {                    // 0x5F is the ONLY special byte
              cap = true;
              b.remove(i);                     // erase(i,1)
              continue;                        // C++ does i -= 1 (size_t wrap ok) then i += 1
          }
          if cap {
              // toupper() in the C locale, called on the SIGN-EXTENDED byte (movsbl).
              // Effect: 0x61..0x7A -> minus 0x20; EVERY other byte, including 0x80..0xFF,
              // is returned unchanged.
              if b[i].is_ascii_lowercase() { b[i] -= 32; }
              cap = false;                     // cleared even if toupper was a no-op
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      // Only 0x61..0x7A were remapped to 0x41..0x5A and only 0x5F bytes removed,
      // so UTF-8 validity is preserved for &str input.
      String::from_utf8(b).unwrap()
  }

=== INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED CLAIMS AND THE PROBES THAT CONFIRMED THEM ===

Claim 1+2 (only 0x5F is a separator; nothing else triggers capitalization):
  EXHAUSTIVE SWEEP A: input "x<byte>y" for every byte 0x01..0xFF except 0x0A (254 probes).
  Output was byte-identical to the input in ALL cases except 0x5F ("x_y" -> "xY"). So '-', ' ',
  '.', '/', ':', tab, '~', digits, 0x7F, and all 0x80..0xFF are copied verbatim and do not set
  the cap flag. Confirmed: a/b_c -> a/bC, a::b_c -> a::bC, ab::cd_ef -> ab::cdEf,
  active_record/errors -> activeRecord/errors (NO Rails-style '/' -> '::' conversion),
  my-word -> my-word / My-word, a.b_c -> a.bC, a b_c -> a bC, "*_?" -> "*?".

Claim 7+9 (toupper is ASCII-only, identity for everything else):
  EXHAUSTIVE SWEEP B: input "_<byte>" for every byte 0x01..0xFF except 0x0A (254 probes).
  Result was exactly <byte> for every value EXCEPT 0x61..0x7A which became 0x41..0x5A, and
  0x5F which vanished. Notably 0x80..0xFF all pass through unchanged (no Latin-1 uppercasing):
  "_\xe9" -> "\xe9", "_\xff" -> "\xff", "_\xd0\xb0" -> "\xd0\xb0".
  Multibyte: é_a -> éA, a_é -> aé / Aé, ß_x -> ßX, U+1E9E ẞ_x -> ẞX, Ünder_score -> ÜnderScore,
  _ölaf -> "\xc3\xb6laf" (0xC3 unchanged), Ä_ä -> Ää.
  Non-letter after '_': _1a -> 1a, 1_2 -> 12, "_-x" -> "-x", "_ x" -> " x", "_\t" -> "\t",
  "$a_b" -> "$aB", "`a`_b" -> "`a`B".

Claim 3 (nothing is ever lowercased):
  Disassembly of 0x406262..0x40636D contains exactly one ctype call: toupper@plt at 0x40631B.
  There is NO tolower call inside camelize (tolower IS imported by the binary, but only for
  downcase/decapitalize). Behaviorally: CamelCase -> CamelCase (both bools), UPPER -> UPPER,
  UPPER_CASE -> UPPERCASE, FOO_bar -> FOOBar, ZZ_zz -> ZZZz, Z_z_Z -> ZZZ,
  ActiveRecord -> ActiveRecord, HTMLParser_x -> HTMLParserX. So lower_first=true means
  "do not uppercase byte 0", NOT "lowercase byte 0".

Claim 4 (the bool only seeds `cap`; variants differ in at most byte 0):
  Machine-checked over the 250-case random differential run: 0 length differences and 0 cases
  where result[1..] differed between the two bools. Identical-output cases confirmed whenever
  byte 0 is '_' or is not in 0x61..0x7A: _leading -> Leading/Leading, _A -> A/A, _id -> Id/Id,
  1_2 -> 12/12, " _a" -> " A"/" A", "$a_b" -> "$aB"/"$aB", Ä_ä -> Ää/Ää, é_a -> éA/éA,
  HTML_tag -> HTMLTag/HTMLTag.

Claim 5+6 (underscore edge cases):
  "" -> ""/""; "_" -> ""/""; "__" -> ""/""; "___" -> ""/""; 40 consecutive '_' -> ""/"".
  _a -> A/A; a_ -> a/A; z_ -> z/Z; ab_cd_ -> abCd/AbCd; user_id_ -> userId/UserId;
  a__b -> aB/AB; x__y__z -> xYZ/XYZ; __double__ -> Double/Double;
  "___ab_____cd__" -> AbCd/AbCd; a_b_c_d_e -> aBCDE/ABCDE;
  ("a_" repeated 60x) -> "a" + "A"x59 (loop shrink is correct; no read past end).

Claim 8 (acronym table NOT consulted):
  html_tag -> htmlTag/HtmlTag; api_key -> apiKey/ApiKey; xml -> xml/Xml; json_data ->
  jsonData/JsonData; http_request -> httpRequest/HttpRequest; my_html_parser ->
  myHtmlParser/MyHtmlParser; html/api/json/http -> html/Html, api/Api, json/Json, http/Http;
  HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API -> unchanged for both bools; API_KEY -> APIKEY/APIKEY;
  Html_tag -> HtmlTag/HtmlTag; tag_html -> tagHtml/TagHtml; my_HTML_tag -> myHTMLTag/MyHTMLTag.

Claim 9 addendum (locale-independence) — I strengthened the evidence:
  `objdump -T` / `nm -D` show the ONLY ctype imports are toupper and tolower; there is NO
  setlocale symbol at all, so the program can never leave the C locale. Behavioral check with
  LC_ALL/LANG set to C, POSIX, tr_TR.UTF-8, tr_TR.utf8, en_US.ISO-8859-1, de_DE.utf8,
  lt_LT.utf8: "i_i" -> iI/II in every one (no dotted-I), "_\xe9" -> "\xe9" in every one
  (no Latin-1 0xC9), "_ölaf" byte-identical in every one.

Claim 10+11: invalid UTF-8 and lone continuation bytes pass through untouched (sweeps A and B
  plus 200 random 1-40-byte strings drawn uniformly from 0x01..0xFF with 25% '_' injection:
  0 mismatches). 0x00 is untestable through argv; the disassembly compares only against 0x5F
  and calls toupper, so NUL would be an ordinary byte.

Newline handling verified separately (line-oriented output makes sed unreliable, so I hexdumped
the whole 11-line output): "a_\n b" i.e. 61 5F 0A 62 -> camelize(true) = 61 0A 62 ("a\nb"),
camelize(false) = 41 0A 62; "\n_x" -> 0A 58 for BOTH bools. So 0x0A is an ordinary byte and
toupper(0x0A) is identity while still clearing cap.

DISASSEMBLY CORROBORATION (0x406262-0x40636D), matching the spec line-for-line:
  0x406286 copy-construct result from the argument (byte-for-byte)
  0x40628B-0x406292 movzbl bool; xor $0x1; store cap byte
  0x406295 i = 0
  0x40629D-0x4062AD call size() EVERY iteration, compare i < size (setb, unsigned)
  0x4062CE cmp $0x5F  -- the single special-byte comparison in the whole function
  0x4062EE call erase(i, 1); 0x4062F3 subq $0x1, i  (size_t underflow when i==0, benign)
  0x4062FA cmpb $0x0, cap
  0x406316 movsbl (sign-extend) then 0x40631B call toupper; 0x406337 store back; 0x406339 cap=0
  0x40633D addq $0x1, i; jmp back to the size() reload
  No regex, no table lookup, no tolower, no acronym access, no setlocale.

RUST NOTE: implement over Vec<u8>. `s.chars()` + `to_uppercase()` is WRONG (it would turn
'é' after '_' into 'É' and 'ß' into "SS", changing length). A literal `i -= 1` panics in debug;
use `remove(i); continue;`.
gotchas: lower_first=true does NOT lowercase anything; there is no tolower call in camelize (verified in disassembly 0x406262-0x40636D). camelize("CamelCase", true) == "CamelCase", not "camelCase".
The acronym table (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) is never consulted: html_tag -> htmlTag/HtmlTag, API_KEY -> APIKEY. Do not add acronym handling.
Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Use Vec<u8>. Rust `chars()` + `to_uppercase()` breaks multibyte: 'é' after '_' must stay C3 A9, and 'ß' must NOT become "SS" (that would change the byte length).
toupper is called on the SIGN-EXTENDED byte (movsbl) so 0x80..0xFF arrive negative; glibc's C-locale table returns them unchanged. Use u8::is_ascii_lowercase / -32, never Unicode uppercasing.

No setlocale symbol exists in the binary (checked with nm -D and objdump -T), so the a-z -> A-Z mapping is fixed regardless of LC_ALL/LANG. Verified across C, POSIX, tr_TR.UTF-8, en_US.ISO-8859-1, de_DE.utf8, lt_LT.utf8.

0x5F ('_') is the ONLY separator. An exhaustive sweep of "x<byte>y" over 0x01..0xFF found 0x5F to be the sole byte that changes anything. '-', ' ', '.', '/', ':', tab, newline, digits are inert. No Rails-style '/' -> '::' conversion.

The C++ does `erase(i,1); i -= 1;` on a size_t: when i == 0 this wraps to SIZE_MAX and the trailing `i += 1` brings it back to 0. In Rust write `b.remove(i); continue;` — a literal `i -= 1` panics on underflow in debug builds.
size() is re-read every iteration, so the loop bound shrinks as underscores are erased. Do not cache the length.
Trailing underscores leave cap=true dangling and it is discarded. "a_" -> "a" / "A"; nothing is appended.
Empty input, all-underscore input, and any input whose first byte is '_' produce BYTE-IDENTICAL output for both bool values.
cap is cleared even when toupper is a no-op, so only the byte immediately after an underscore run is a candidate for uppercasing. "_1a" -> "1a" (the 'a' stays lowercase), "_-x" -> "-x".

The two bool variants can differ ONLY in byte 0 of the result, and only when byte 0 is ASCII a-z. Verified mechanically over 250 random cases (0 tail differences). Don't assume a general transform between them.

0x0A is an ordinary byte: "a_
b" -> "a
b" (the '
' absorbs the cap flag, so 'b' stays lowercase). Watch out when testing via `sed -n '3p'` — newlines in the word shift the 11-line output.
Invalid UTF-8 and lone continuation bytes pass through byte-for-byte, so a &[u8] implementation is exactly equivalent; from_utf8 on the result of a valid &str input is guaranteed to succeed.
unresolved: Behavior for a 0x00 byte inside the word cannot be observed (argv is NUL-terminated). The disassembly compares only against 0x5F and calls toupper, so 0x00 would be an ordinary inert byte — but this is inference, not observation. Irrelevant for Rust &str anyway.
The bool is read with movzbl then xor $0x1, so a caller passing a bool byte other than 0/1 (e.g. 2) would yield cap=3 (truthy) — unreachable from this CLI and from well-formed C++.
Extremely large inputs (megabytes) were not tested; argv length limits cap this. The algorithm is O(n^2) in the worst case (erase shifts the tail) but behaviorally identical.
